prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength free of first-order light shift and motional broadening, taking optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B022 with Katori and Ye. After reading the full exchange I am more confident, not because five members agree, but because the objections raised against it have narrowed to two that can be tested against the record. First, distinctness from 2005 and 2012. The comb prize rewarded a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize rewarded control of a single quantum system. The magic-wavelength lattice is a different invention: it makes the light shift cancel to first order for the clock transition, so thousands of atoms can be held tightly (Lamb-Dicke regime) and read out together, which is what moves the statistical limit and the systematic limit down at once. That was not an obvious outcome, and the citation should state exactly that. Second, the verification. Clock-to-clock agreement at about 1e-18 between independent laboratories and over fibre links is the kind of direct experimental verification I require, and it is already producing physics, such as the redshift resolved over millimetres in a single cloud. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: the concept and first realisation with Sr on one side, the demonstrated accuracy and stability frontier and many-body control on the other. The committee's mandate is a discovery or invention, and I regard this as an invention with a verified, growing consequence.
statement.case_against: The two real weaknesses remain. The overlap with 2005 and 2012 can be answered by wording but not removed, and a colleague who reads the lattice clock as an instrument refinement will not be convinced by wording alone. And two names leave out people who made real contributions to the early lattice work, such as Takamoto (Katori's own group), Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Ovsiannikov. I am relying on memory for the exact order of the early strontium papers and the first magic-wavelength demonstrations, and I would not want to finalise the names until the committee's experts have documented that sequence. A smaller point is that the second has not been redefined, but I treat that as irrelevant to the scientific case.

responses.point: Kroll treats Takamoto's work as covered by Katori and regards the two-name credit as clean, with a citation that rewards the lattice concept and its realisation rather than clocks in general.
responses.response: I agree on the citation principle and I now think Kroll is right about Takamoto in practice: he was a member of Katori's group and the Nobel record in such cases usually credits the group leader who conceived the experiment. That is a position on conception and leadership, though, and I want it verified from the first papers, not assumed. I still do not think Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley can be set aside on the same argument, since they led separate groups. My answer is that Katori is credited for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for the performance and many-body frontier, and that the committee should request documentation of that sequence before the final ballot. If the documents show it, I am comfortable with two names.

responses.point: Danielsson asks whether a clock tells us something unexpected about nature, rather than giving limits on drifting constants and dark matter, and prefers B002 as a clean clue from the universe, though he says he would not block B022.
responses.response: I take the distinction seriously, but I think the answer is that the prize here is for a new capability that produced observations, not for a null search. Many atoms can be interrogated without a first-order shift or motional broadening, which was not known to be possible before it was done, and the millimetre-scale redshift is a positive measurement of nature. I also disagree gently on BAO. His own argument that the theory of the feature predates the 2005 detection, and that two survey collaborations found it, is exactly why I cannot be absolutely sure that a trio identifies the original work. I accept that DESI may sharpen the importance of BAO, but that does not repair the credit, and a third cosmology prize in twenty years adds a second reservation.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for B045 but names B022 as his first alternative and says he would sooner see it awarded cleanly than force a contested trio.
responses.response: I am grateful for that statement, and it is where the committee can make progress. I accept his objection to my round-1 trio: dropping Mele removes half of the Z2 theory, and I withdraw the suggestion that Hasan should replace him. My remaining concern is about the unit, not the people: a quantum spin Hall prize rests on an experiment in HgTe that followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, whose author Zhang is deceased and outside any trio, and the 3D ARPES work then lies outside the citation. If the committee wanted B045 I could support Kane, Mele and Molenkamp with an explicit 2D framing. But he has said the credit cannot be settled, and I would then be glad to see B022 done without delay.

responses.point: Mehlig describes the lattice clock as an application of known atomic physics, and says conceptual novelty in a classifying invariant should rank above a smaller uncertainty budget, while granting that B022 is the safer prize.
responses.response: I do not think the lattice clock is merely the application of known physics. Magic-wavelength trapping and Lamb-Dicke confinement were known as ingredients, but showing that a closed-shell atom has a wavelength at which both clock levels shift equally, and that this survives with thousands of atoms in a real apparatus, is a design that had to be conceived and then demonstrated. It is the combination that is new. I accept his point that B045 has a stronger conceptual classification, and for that reason I keep it as my first alternative. But his own statement that B022 is the safer prize if uncontested allocation is weighted above field-level influence matches my own priority under the mandate.

responses.point: Pearce has moved from IceCube to B022, concedes that independent confirmation of B046 from another detector is thinner, and accepts that the lattice-clock citation must say precisely what is new.
responses.response: I appreciate that he has been willing to move and I agree with the citation point. I would not weaken the wording by saying precision clocks in general. On B046 I stay where I was: the diffuse flux is real, but source identification is limited and two names still sit uneasily against a collaboration of several hundred people and the AMANDA precursor. If he can supply documentation of the decisive individual roles I would reconsider it for a future year, but I would not put it above B022 now.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B022 for its cross-laboratory reproducibility and clean attribution, and says the novelty objection is a judgment call, with the redefinition of the second not yet done.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and on the judgment call, and I would add that the committee should not hide behind it: it should write the distinction from 2005 and 2012 into the citation and defend it. On his declared conflict, I note that he has said he will step back from the B039 discussion, which is the right course, and I do not see his interest as touching B022. On waiting for the redefinition, I would say that the discovery and its verification are already complete, and that the redefinition follows from them.

uncertainties: Whether the documented early record (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock, the sequence of Ye's accuracy results and the early work of Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley) fully supports Katori for concept and first demonstration and Ye for the performance frontier; I rely on memory and want expert documentation.
Whether the committee as a whole accepts the lattice clock as a distinct invention from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and not as a refinement.
Whether Kroll's or others' view of Takamoto as covered by Katori survives a reading of the first papers.
If B045 is chosen instead, whether Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leaves out the 3D experiments and the BHZ proposal to an extent that makes the citation look arbitrary.
statement.conflict_note: No documented personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist, and no co-authorship with any of them. I note Johansson's declared interest in B039 and B032 (he is a Chalmers colleague), and Kroll's declared connection to Hall's laboratory, which I do not consider disqualifying for B022 though it should be recorded. I have no conflict to add since round 1.
